title: FeMoCo ground-state energy resource estimate via Trotter-based phase estimation (Reiher et al., 2017)
headline: FeMoCo's ground-state energy could be computed to 0.1 mHa in about 130 days with 111 logical qubits and 1.1 × 10¹⁵ T gates, or about 180 million physical qubits at a 10⁻³ error rate.

source.title: Elucidating reaction mechanisms on quantum computers

venue.name: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

assertion.what_is_claimed: Computing the ground-state energy of FeMoCo structure 1 (54 electrons in 54 spatial orbitals, spin 0, charge +3) to 0.1 mHa by phase estimation on a second-order Trotter–Suzuki step, with rotations executed serially, needs about 1.1e15 T gates and 111 logical qubits, and takes about 130 days at one logical T gate per 10 ns (Table 1). With the surface code and physical gates at 100 MHz, the same computation needs about 1.8e8 physical qubits at a physical error rate of 1e-3 and about 1.2e6 at 1e-6 (Table 2).
assertion.method: Second-order Trotter–Suzuki product formula in the Jordan–Wigner representation, with phase estimation, serial term ordering, and repeat-until-success synthesis of rotations into Clifford and T gates
assertion.architecture_assumed: Surface code with 15-to-1 magic-state distillation in dedicated T factories, physical gates at 100 MHz, and one logical T gate every 10 ns

code_distance.note: Stated as "35,17"; the second distance is not explained in the table

trotter_number.note: Steps per inverse hartree for a Trotter error of 0.1 mHa, extrapolated from small molecules

synthesis_t_gates_offset.locator: arXiv:1605.03590v2, Eq. A5 and Table IV

assessment.summary_plain: QAC rebuilt the estimate from the paper's own FeMoCo integrals and cost formula. The logical qubit count agrees: 110 against 111. The T count does not: we obtain 1.14 × 10¹⁶ against the paper's 1.1 × 10¹⁵, a factor of 10.4×. With a lattice-surgery surface-code model in place of the paper's, the machine needs 2.72 million physical qubits but about 449 years.
what_this_shows: The paper's logical qubit count follows from its stated ingredients, to within one qubit.
The Jordan–Wigner Hamiltonian built from the paper's integrals has about twice as many Pauli terms as the term count the paper's cost formula uses.
The paper's cost formula, evaluated with the paper's own constants and term count, gives several times more T gates than the paper's tables report.
The physical cost depends strongly on how fast logical T gates can be applied; a lattice-surgery model gives a much smaller but much slower machine than the paper's.
what_this_does_not_show: It does not establish which of the paper's figures or inputs is the source of the T-count difference; the paper's circuits and scripts are not public.
The Trotter number, which sets the number of Trotter steps, is taken from the paper and was not rebuilt.
The full 54-orbital circuit was not compiled; its rotation count comes from a term count and a per-step rule checked on smaller active spaces.
The paper's surface-code model was not rebuilt, so the physical comparison is not like-for-like.
Preparing the trial state is not costed, as in the paper.

findings.note: Spin orbitals, one phase-estimation qubit, and the one synthesis ancilla the paper mentions; the paper lists one more qubit without a breakdown.
About twice the rotations per Trotter step, and the paper's formula does not return its tabulated count even with its own inputs.
Computed with a lattice-surgery model that applies T gates far more slowly, so far fewer T factories are needed.
Computed with a logical cycle per T gate where the paper assumes one T gate per physical gate time, on top of the larger T count.
Selected by the resource estimator for a longer computation than the paper's.

assessment.classical_status_note: Not assessed in this reproduction. The record for the same active space, femoco-low-2025, lists not_solved_classically_at_target_accuracy with a review pending.

tool.name: QDK Chemistry and the QDK resource estimator
tool.role: QDK Chemistry maps the paper's FeMoCo integrals to Pauli terms on truncated active spaces and compiles second-order Trotter steps for them, which fixes the rotation count per step; the paper's cost formula turns that count into Trotter steps and T gates; the QDK resource estimator converts the logical counts into physical qubits and runtime.

deviations_from_reported.reported: The cost formula (Eq. E2) uses twice the paper's own count of Hamiltonian terms for the 54-orbital basis, quoted in Appendix E without a derivation
deviations_from_reported.used: Every Pauli term of the Jordan–Wigner Hamiltonian built from the paper's integrals, counted with a closed form that matches the QDK Chemistry qubit mapper term for term on truncated active spaces
deviations_from_reported.why: The paper's formula treats each term as one single-qubit rotation, and each Pauli term needs one rotation. We could not determine how the paper's smaller count was obtained, and thresholding small terms does not reproduce it.

deviations_from_reported.reported: The full Trotter circuit was built in LIQUi|> and its gates were counted
deviations_from_reported.used: Second-order Trotter steps compiled by QDK Chemistry for truncated active spaces of the same integrals; the rotation count of the full step follows from the Pauli-term count by a rule that holds exactly for every compiled circuit
deviations_from_reported.why: LIQUi|> and the paper's circuits are not public, and compiling the full step in QDK Chemistry needs more memory than a laptop has.

deviations_from_reported.reported: The split among phase estimation, Trotter error, and synthesis is found by calculus on a simplified cost (Eq. E3) and then used in Eq. E2
deviations_from_reported.used: The same simplified cost is minimized on a fixed grid of budget fractions, and the T gates per rotation are rounded to three decimals
deviations_from_reported.why: A fixed grid and fixed rounding make the result identical on every platform, which the registry's weekly rerun requires. The effect on the T count is far below one percent.

deviations_from_reported.reported: A total for the serial case, without a breakdown
deviations_from_reported.used: The spin orbitals, one phase-estimation qubit, and the one ancilla the paper says its rotation synthesis needs
deviations_from_reported.why: These are the qubits the paper's text accounts for. The paper's total is one higher.

deviations_from_reported.reported: A surface-code costing that follows the paper's Ref. 48, with a main processor and dedicated T factories
deviations_from_reported.used: The QDK resource estimator with the rotated surface code, lattice surgery, and round-based 15-to-1 T factories
deviations_from_reported.why: These are the models available in the resource estimator. The paper gives the outputs of its costing but not enough of the model to rebuild it.

Horsman et al., Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery

deviations_from_reported.reported: One logical T gate every 10 ns, the same as the physical gate time, with enough T factories to supply that rate
deviations_from_reported.used: One logical cycle per T state, that is, a code distance's worth of syndrome-extraction rounds
deviations_from_reported.why: The lattice-surgery model of the resource estimator has no faster mode. This is the main reason the physical figures differ from the paper's in both directions.

deviations_from_reported.aspect: Rotation synthesis in the physical estimate
deviations_from_reported.reported: Repeat-until-success synthesis with the average T cost of Eq. A5
deviations_from_reported.used: PSSPC synthesis, searching up to eighty T states per rotation instead of the default maximum of twenty
deviations_from_reported.why: The resource estimator synthesizes rotations this way. With the default range no configuration meets the error budget for this many rotations. The logical T count reported here still uses the paper's Eq. A5.

deviations_from_reported.reported: Not stated; physical gates take 10 ns
deviations_from_reported.used: Measurements take the same time as gates
deviations_from_reported.why: The resource estimator needs a measurement time, and the paper gives a single physical time scale.

deviations_from_reported.used: A total failure probability of one percent for the whole run
deviations_from_reported.why: The resource estimator needs an error budget. One percent is the value used in the registry's existing FeMoCo record.

deviations_from_reported.reported: Stated in Table 2 as an outcome of the paper's analysis
deviations_from_reported.used: Chosen by the resource estimator, taking the trade-off with the smallest product of physical qubits and runtime
deviations_from_reported.why: The resource estimator returns several trade-offs between qubits and runtime; a fixed rule is needed to pick one.

deviations_from_reported.aspect: Estimating one Trotter step at a time
deviations_from_reported.used: The resource estimator costs one Trotter step with the failure budget divided by the number of steps, and the runtime is multiplied by the number of steps
deviations_from_reported.why: The resource estimator stores runtime as a 64-bit count of nanoseconds, which overflows for a computation this long. The notebook checks on a shorter run that both ways give the same machine.

interpretation.label: inconsistent
interpretation.statement: The logical qubit count is reproduced, but the T count is not. Our count is about an order of magnitude above the paper's, and the difference has two identified parts. The Jordan–Wigner Hamiltonian built from the paper's integrals has about twice as many Pauli terms as the term count in the paper's formula. Separately, the paper's formula evaluated with the paper's own constants and term count gives several times more T gates than the paper's tables. We did not find the cause of either and did not adjust inputs to remove them. The physical estimates use a lattice-surgery model in which a T gate takes a logical cycle; the paper assumes a T gate per physical gate time. That choice alone makes our machine much smaller and much slower than the paper's, so the physical comparison shows the dependence on architecture and does not test the paper's Table 2.

notes: The Trotter number, which fixes the number of Trotter steps, is taken from the paper's Table IV. The paper obtains it by rescaling a rigorous bound with data from small molecules, and that calculation is not rebuilt here.

Phase estimation is costed as in the paper's Lemma 2, in which the control qubit flips the sign of each rotation through Clifford gates, so a controlled step has as many rotations as an uncontrolled one. QDK Chemistry's stock controlled mapper uses two rotations per term; the notebook shows both counts.
The integrals are the paper's original structure-1 file, fetched from a pinned commit of microsoft/qdk-chemistry-data and checked against a SHA-256 digest before use.
The resource estimator is given the qubits the Trotter circuit uses, without the paper's synthesis ancilla, because PSSPC synthesis accounts for its own workspace.

The runtime compared with the paper is the physical runtime of the headline scenario. The runtime at the paper's own rate of one logical T gate per 10 ns is recorded in results.json as runtime_seconds_at_logical_t_rate.

narrative_markdown:
# Reproducing the FeMoCo resource estimate of Reiher et al. (2017)

*Yash Kumar, Jolin Wang, and Daniel Ng (PlexTech, UC Berkeley), for the Quantum Applications Center, UW–Madison.*
*Numbers in this page are rendered from the claim record; the record's numbers come from the executed notebook in `reproductions/qdk-trotter-2026-11/`.*

## The claim

[Reiher et al. (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1619152114) gave the first detailed estimate of what it
would take to compute the ground-state energy of FeMoCo, the iron–molybdenum cofactor of nitrogenase, on a
quantum computer. Their active space, 54 electrons in
54 orbitals, became the standard benchmark for later algorithms.
Read literally, the paper claims:

> FeMoCo's ground-state energy could be computed to 0.1 mHa in about 130 days with 111 logical qubits and 1.1 × 10¹⁵ T gates, or about 180 million physical qubits at a 10⁻³ error rate.

The algorithm is the simplest one available. The Hamiltonian is mapped to qubits with the Jordan–Wigner
transformation, its time evolution is approximated by second-order Trotter–Suzuki steps, and phase estimation
reads the energy from those steps. Two layers of numbers sit behind the claim.

**Logical counts.** For a total error of 0.0001 Ha, with
rotations executed one at a time, Table 1 reports about 1.1 × 10¹⁵ T gates and
111 logical qubits. At one logical T gate every
10 ns that is 130 days.
The preprint's appendices give the cost formula behind the T count (Eq. E2) and its inputs: a count of
6.1 × 10⁶ Hamiltonian terms, a Trotter number of
166 extrapolated from small molecules, and an average of
1.15 log₂(1/ε) + 9.2
T gates to synthesize a rotation to accuracy ε.

**Physical resources.** Table 2 adds the surface code, with physical gates of
10 ns and enough T factories to keep to the runtime of
Table 1. At a physical error rate of 1 × 10⁻³ it lists
202 T factories, code distance
35, and about 180 million physical
qubits; at an error rate of 1 × 10⁻⁶ the total falls to about
1.2 million.

## What QAC did

We rebuilt the estimate with [QDK Chemistry](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry)
(version 2.3.0) and the resource estimator in the
[QDK](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk) (version 1.33.1). The
[executed notebook](https://github.com/QuantumApplicationsCenter/qac-claims/blob/main/claims/femoco-reiher-2017/reproductions/qdk-trotter-2026-11/notebook.ipynb)
walks through every step.

**The paper's own Hamiltonian.** The integrals are the original structure-1 file of Reiher et al., which
Microsoft publishes with the first author's permission in
[qdk-chemistry-data](https://github.com/microsoft/qdk-chemistry-data/tree/main/data/hamiltonians/FeMoco-Reiher2017).
The notebook downloads it from a pinned commit and checks its SHA-256 digest. Unlike the registry's other
FeMoCo record, nothing here is synthetic.

**Pauli terms.** The cost of a Trotter step is set by the number of Pauli terms in the Jordan–Wigner
Hamiltonian. We count them with a closed form and check it against QDK Chemistry's qubit mapper, which returns
the same terms with the same coefficients on truncated active spaces of up to
8 orbitals. The full
Hamiltonian has 12,604,410 Pauli terms. That is
2.1× the
6.1 × 10⁶ terms the paper quotes. Discarding small terms does
not close the difference, and we could not determine how the paper's count was obtained.

**Rotations per Trotter step.** QDK Chemistry compiles a second-order Trotter step into one rotation per Pauli
exponential, and the notebook confirms the count on circuits compiled for the truncated active spaces. For
FeMoCo a step has 25,208,819 rotations. The full circuit is
too large to compile on a laptop, so this figure follows from the term count and the rule checked on the smaller
circuits. Phase estimation is costed as in the paper's Lemma 2, which controls a step with Clifford gates and
adds no rotations.

**Trotter steps and T gates.** We then apply the paper's Eq. E2 with the paper's constants. The Trotter number
is the one input we take on trust: the paper extrapolates it from molecules small enough to simulate, and we
did not repeat that. The result is 6,861,089 Trotter steps,
1.73 × 10¹⁴ rotations at
65.886 T gates each, and
1.14 × 10¹⁶ T gates in total, on
110 logical qubits. At the paper's rate of one T gate per
10 ns that is
1318.9 days.

**Physical resources.** The QDK resource estimator takes these logical counts with the paper's stated
assumptions (physical gates of 10 ns, the surface
code, 15-to-1 distillation) and its own lattice-surgery model for the rest. At an error rate of
1 × 10⁻³ it returns
2.72 million physical qubits
(2,721,009) at code distance
39, with
15 T factories, and a runtime of about
449 years. At an error rate of
1 × 10⁻⁶ it returns
181,529 physical qubits at distance
9 and about
104 years.

## How to read the comparison

**The logical qubit count agrees.** We count 110 qubits from
the ingredients the paper names: the spin orbitals, one phase-estimation qubit, and one ancilla for rotation
synthesis. The paper lists 111 without a breakdown.

**The T count does not.** Ours is 10.4× the paper's. The notebook separates
the difference into two parts.

- *Rotations per step.* Using every Pauli term instead of the paper's term count raises the T count by
  2.1×.
- *The formula against the tables.* Eq. E2, evaluated with the paper's own term count and the constants of its
  Table IV, gives 5.41 × 10¹⁵ T gates. Table 1 reports
  1.1 × 10¹⁵. With the three errors added linearly, as in Table IV, the formula
  gives 5.74 × 10¹⁵ against the table's
  1.2 × 10¹⁵.

We did not find the cause of either part, and we did not change any input to make the numbers agree. The
second part does not involve our Hamiltonian or our tools: it compares the paper's formula with the paper's
tables. The paper's circuits and scripts are not public, so an unstated step in its calculation may account for
it.

**The physical figures differ in both directions, for one reason.** The paper sizes its machine to apply a
logical T gate every 10 ns, which takes
202 T factories, and those factories hold almost all of its qubits.
In the lattice-surgery model a T gate takes a logical cycle, here
2,340 ns. Far fewer factories keep up
at that pace, so our machine has 98% fewer qubits than the
paper's and runs about 1,261 times as long. The runtime ratio combines the
slower T gates with the larger T count. Neither figure tests the paper's Table 2, because the model is
different.

## What this does not show, and what comes next

- It does not show which of the paper's numbers is the source of the T-count difference. A count of the
  rotations in the paper's original circuits, or the script behind its Table IV, would settle it.
- It does not rebuild the Trotter number. A tighter or looser value would change the T count in proportion.
- It does not compile the full 54-orbital circuit; the largest compiled
  check uses 8 orbitals.
- It does not reproduce the paper's surface-code model. A like-for-like physical comparison needs a model in
  which T gates are applied as fast as the paper assumes.
- It covers the serial ordering at 0.0001 Ha only. Table 1 also
  gives a 1 mHa case and the nesting and PAR orderings, which are natural later variants.

## Reproducing this result

The [notebook](https://github.com/QuantumApplicationsCenter/qac-claims/blob/main/claims/femoco-reiher-2017/reproductions/qdk-trotter-2026-11/notebook.ipynb)
runs in about 31 seconds on a laptop, in the environment pinned by
`requirements.lock.txt` (Python 3.10.22). It downloads the integral file
on first use, so it needs a network connection. From a checkout of this repository:

```bash
python3.10 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r claims/femoco-reiher-2017/reproductions/qdk-trotter-2026-11/requirements.lock.txt
pip install -e ".[execute]"
qacclaims execute claims/femoco-reiher-2017/reproductions/qdk-trotter-2026-11
```

The last command re-executes the notebook and reports any difference from the committed `results.json`.
